brief.summary: A library of recorded lab meetings for academic research groups, with transcripts, speaker labels and topic chapters, so members who missed meetings can catch up by listening.
brief.user: Dr. Okonkwo, a postdoctoral researcher in a 14-person coastal ecology lab who just got back from three weeks of fieldwork on a research vessel with almost no internet.

She also needs to know what to listen to next and what she can skip.

prompt:
I need the front end for Labminutes. A library of recorded lab meetings for academic research groups, with transcripts, speaker labels and topic chapters, so members who missed meetings can catch up by listening.

Who's using it: Dr. Okonkwo, a postdoctoral researcher in a 14-person coastal ecology lab who just got back from three weeks of fieldwork on a research vessel with almost no internet.

What they're doing right now: She missed three weekly lab meetings and two journal clubs, and on Thursday she has to present her cruise data plan. In between, the lab apparently changed how it shares time on the flow cytometer and argued about authorship order on a group manuscript she's on. She's listening at 1.5x speed on her commute, jumping to the parts that matter to her, slowing down when the PI is explaining a decision, and replaying the 90 seconds where her name came up. She also needs to know what to listen to next and what she can skip.

What's in the system at this point: Recordings from the past 5 weeks: lab meetings on Oct 15, Oct 22, Oct 29 and Nov 5 (52–78 min each) and journal clubs on Oct 24 and Nov 7 (41 and 37 min). Each has a machine transcript (about 9,000–13,000 words), speaker labels for 11 identified people (PI Prof. Halvorsen, lab manager Jun Takeda, grad students Ama, Ruiz and Becker, etc.) and chapters such as 'Cytometer booking rules — 14 min', 'Manuscript: Kelp forest recovery — authorship', 'Cruise logistics'. Her name is mentioned 6 times across 3 recordings. 9 action items were captured, 2 assigned to her. She has already listened to the Oct 15 meeting up to 23:40, and her saved speed is 1.5x.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
